one_line: Yugabyte's CEO argues agent memory is solved but cross-agent learning is not, and demos Mako, a private-to-shared context store where humans promote memories and provenance is traceable.
summary: The speaker, a Yugabyte co-founder, says per-agent memory works but learning across a group of agents is unsolved. He says handoffs through output files (MD, PDF) lose the reasoning and dead ends, so the receiving agent re-derives everything and burns tokens. He lists five misconceptions: more memory is not learning, shared files are not shared knowledge, RAG over everything is not quality, fine-tuning cannot persist lessons, and bigger context windows make context rot worse. He describes their failed attempts (a distributed RAG pipeline, per-agent Postgres, a headless backend with no human in the loop) and the tuning that followed. The product pitch is Mako, which stores private memories, promotes selected pieces to a shared space under human supervision, and records provenance and traces. A recorded, sped-up demo shows cross-session resumability and cross-IDE sharing via MCP tool calls. Most claims are vendor-side and the metrics are only partly specified, so treat the numbers as self-reported.

key_ideas.idea: Per-agent memory is solved, but learning across a group of agents is not, and single-agent memory infrastructure is not the same as what shared learning needs.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker frames the gap as an infrastructure problem: memory is extracted from a single agent's conversations and reused by that agent, while learning requires sharing across agents.

key_ideas.idea: Passing only the output of an agent to another agent loses the reasoning, the dead ends and the failed attempts, so the receiver re-derives the work at token cost.
key_ideas.detail: He compares it to a new team member who needs the project history; without it they re-argue settled decisions.

key_ideas.idea: Five misconceptions: more memory is not learning, shared files are not shared knowledge, RAG over everything is not quality, fine-tuning does not persist lessons, and a bigger context window makes things worse.
key_ideas.detail: He calls each one an architecture gap rather than a feature gap. Context rot is the stated reason larger windows fail.

key_ideas.idea: Shared context needs three properties: agents work on the same context, contributions are supervised (promoted) rather than open, and every fact can be traced to a source, person or conversation.
key_ideas.detail: He compares contribution to code review: not everyone can write to the shared context, and promotion is what makes it durable.

key_ideas.idea: Their own earlier designs failed (a shared knowledge base with a distributed RAG pipeline, per-agent tiny Postgres, a headless backend with no UI), and tuning the RAG stack one variable at a time improved results.
key_ideas.detail: Without a human in the loop they could not see what went wrong. Per-variable tuning from traces raised the reported scores and cut the context from about 7,000 chunks to about 1,000.

key_ideas.idea: Each memory is private by default and is promoted to a shared space one piece at a time, so access is fine-grained rather than whole-store.
key_ideas.detail: In the demo, a memory was invisible to another client until it was promoted, and then it became retrievable. A maintainer can still open a whole data pack.

key_ideas.idea: Human promotion decisions can serve as labeled examples of good memory for future self-improving orchestration, and decision traces down to tool calls can show whether the memory actually saved tokens.
key_ideas.detail: He says the trace lets a team check cost savings instead of assuming them. He presents training on promotions as a future direction, not something shipped.

key_ideas.idea: Shared incident memory stops many agents from repeatedly calling a service that is down, because the first agent to hit the failure records it for the rest.
key_ideas.detail: This is a proposed use case with no measured result in the talk.

techniques.name: Private-to-shared promotion gate
techniques.how: Agents write memories to a private scope. A human or a supervised step promotes selected items into a shared scope, so only reviewed items become shared context.
techniques.when: When several agents or people share context and unreviewed memory would add noise or cost.

techniques.name: Provenance on every memory
techniques.how: Store the source (data source, person or conversation) for each extracted fact so it can be traced back before it is trusted or promoted.
techniques.when: When shared context must be audited or when a wrong fact needs to be traced to its origin.

techniques.name: Scoped data packs with a skill-driven MCP interface
techniques.how: Group memories into named packs. Expose create and add operations over MCP, and use a skill to tell the agent when to write, so calls are not made on every turn.
techniques.when: When the same memory must be read from different IDE or chat clients under one account.

techniques.name: Cross-session resumability via shared memory
techniques.how: Start a session, kill it, and start a new one. The new session first searches the stored conversation and then continues, so no project or memory toggle is needed.
techniques.when: When work on a topic spans days or devices and re-deriving prior reasoning costs tokens.

techniques.name: One-variable-at-a-time RAG tuning with traces
techniques.how: Change a single retrieval variable, re-run with tracing, and keep only changes that improve the metric. Track context chunk count as well as precision.
techniques.when: When a RAG pipeline built from best-of-breed components performs poorly and the cause is unknown.

techniques.name: Trace-based token accounting
techniques.how: Inspect stored conversation traces down to the tool call to measure whether a retrieval avoided repeated token spend.
techniques.when: When a team wants evidence that shared memory reduces cost rather than assuming it.

numbers.claim: Initial RAG faithfulness was 14% on an MD benchmark and 20% on a PDF benchmark. Context precision started at 57%.
Scores rose to 65, 74 and then 82 after one-variable-at-a-time tuning. The speaker does not say which metric each value refers to.
Context chunks dropped from over 7,000 to about 1,000 (about one-seventh of the context size), with higher precision and lower token spend.
The speaker says the token savings from resumed sessions are large but gives no measured figure. The demo only shows the mechanism.

hot_takes: Agent memory is solved, but agent learning is not.
Shared state is not shared knowledge.
A bigger context window is the surest way to the quickest, most expensive failure.
Fine-tuning cannot save and persist lessons that agents learn.
Running RAG over every transcript adds garbage and burns more tokens for worse results.

relevance.why: MemoryMesh already has tiered cross-session memory with provenance and conflict resolution. The talk's private-to-shared promotion gate and per-memory traceability map onto that design, and the trace-based token check matches the benchmark-first thesis.
relevance.action: Add a private-to-shared promotion step to MemoryMesh that requires a human or rule-based approval and stores the source reference, then measure chunk count and token use before and after promotion on a fixed task set.

relevance.why: Resumability across sessions is related to ProsHarness checkpoint/resume. The talk's approach is memory search over a shared store, not a checkpoint, so the overlap is partial.
relevance.action: Compare ProsHarness checkpoint/resume with a memory-search resume on the same long run and check which needs fewer tokens to restart.

relevance.why: Stated general principle: shared agent context should be a reviewed, provenance-tagged layer rather than a raw RAG dump. The talk offers no independent evidence.
relevance.action: Read the RAG tuning steps in the talk and check whether our own retrieval changes were tested one variable at a time with traces.
